Get Down
GET DOWN
verb phrase (Boomer slang)
In 1960s–70s African-American and funk slang, get down meant to dance with abandon, to let loose, to enjoy oneself fully, or to get serious about something ("get down to business"). James Brown’s shouts made it famous, KC and the Sunshine Band’s "Get Down Tonight" (No. 1, 1975) made it national, and Kool & the Gang’s "Get Down On It" (1981) kept it going.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To get down is to let loose and enjoy yourself completely — to dance hard, to party, to throw yourself into the moment. "Everybody get down!" The Christian observation: the phrase names a whole-hearted joy, and Scripture is not against whole-hearted joy; it is for it, and it knows where to find it. David got down before the ark, dancing "with all his might," and when his wife Michal sneered at the king acting so undignified, he answered: "I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight" (2Sa 6:22). That is joy that does not care how it looks because it is aimed at God. Nehemiah told a weeping people to go and feast, "for the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Neh 8:10). The Psalmist knew the source: "in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore" (Psa 16:11). Paul commands it outright: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice" (Php 4:4). The funk lyric meant something else — a night of pleasure, often a sexual one. Scripture does not compete with that by being dull; it competes by being deeper. The joy of the Lord is the only joy you can get down to without regret in the morning. A father who laughs loud, sings loud in church, and dances with his daughter at her wedding is showing his children that faith is not a frown.

Webster 1828 Definition

1960s–70s funk slang for dancing hard and enjoying oneself fully ("Get Down Tonight," 1975) — whole-hearted joy that Scripture locates in God’s presence (Psa 16:11) and models in David dancing with all his might (2Sa 6:22).

expand to see more

GET DOWN, v. phr. (African-American and funk slang, 1960s–70s; Boomer era) 1. To dance energetically; to let oneself go. 2. To enjoy oneself fully; to party. 3. To get serious; to apply oneself ("get down to business").

Decode for families: in 1975 lyrics, get down tonight usually meant more than dancing. In a grandparent’s mouth today it usually means dancing.

Key Scripture

2Sa 6:22 — "And I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight: and of the maidservants which thou hast spoken of, of them shall I be had in honour."

Neh 8:10 — "Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength."

Psa 16:11 — "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore."

Php 4:4 — "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice."

Luk 15:24 — "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry."

Modern Corruption

The funk anthem sought whole-hearted joy in a night of pleasure; Scripture offers a deeper whole-hearted joy in God’s presence, with no regrets in the morning.

expand to see more

Much of 1970s pop music was an argument that joy is found in the body, the night, and the moment. "Get down tonight" was its motto. The argument persuaded a generation, and the morning-after cost was paid in broken marriages and broken lives. The Christian should not answer that argument with gloom, as though God were against joy. He should answer it with a better joy.

That better joy has a shape. It is "in thy presence" (Psa 16:11), so it does not fade when the music stops. It is "of the LORD" (Neh 8:10), so it is strength, not weakness. And it is unembarrassed: David danced in front of everyone and did not care what Michal thought (2Sa 6:22). The father in the parable did not send his returning son to a quiet room; "they began to be merry" (Luk 15:24). The gospel is the best reason in the universe to get down.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Get (Old Norse geta) + down → 1960s–70s AAVE / funk get down (dance, let loose) → "Get Down Tonight" (1975).

expand to see more

Old Norse geta — to obtain, to reach; Old English of dúne — off the hill, downward

1960s–70s AAVE and funk: get down — to dance, to let loose, to get serious

James Brown’s stage shouts popularize the phrase

1975: KC and the Sunshine Band, "Get Down Tonight" (No. 1)

Hebrew simchah — joy, gladness (Neh 8:10; Psa 16:11)

Usage

""When the band played Motown at the reception, Grandpa got down. Grandma got down too. The grandkids filmed it.""

"The joy of the LORD is your strength (Neh 8:10)."

"In thy presence is fulness of joy (Psa 16:11)."
